(p-150) **Surah al-Qiyamah (The Resurrection)**

The second: it has entered for the *taʾkīd* (emphasis) of the speech, as in his saying: *lā wallāhi* (no, by God), and as in the words of Imruʾ al-Qays:

*"No, by your father, daughter of al-ʿĀmirī, the people do not claim that I flee."*

This is the view of Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh.

The third: it is a rejection of a previous statement made by the polytheists denying resurrection, and then he began the oath (p-151) saying: "I swear by the Day of Resurrection," to distinguish between a new oath and an oath that is a renewal. This is the view of al-Farrāʾ.

The second: that He swore by the Day of Resurrection and did not swear by the self that blames. This is the view of al-Ḥasan, and the sense of the speech would be: "I swear by the Day of Resurrection, and I do not swear by the self that blames."

One: it is a description of praise, and this is the view of those who considered it an oath.

The second: it is a description of blame, and this is the view of those who denied that it is an oath.

The first: it is the one that blames itself for what has passed and regrets it. This is the view of Mujāhid: it blames itself for evil, asking why it did it, and for good, asking why it did not increase it.

The second: it is the one that possesses blame (*dhāt al-lawm*). This is related from Ibn ʿĪsā.

The third: it is the one that blames itself for what it blames others for.

According to these three interpretations, *al-lawwāmah* means *al-lāʾimah* (the one that blames).

As for those who took it as a description of blame, they have three interpretations of it:

The first: it is the blameworthy one. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās.

The second: it is the one that is blamed for the evil it has done.

The third: it is the one that has no patience with the trials and hardships of this world, so it blames a great deal within it. According to these three interpretations, *al-lawwāmah* means *al-malūmah* (the one that is blamed).

﴿Ayaḥsabu l-insānu﴾ (*Does man think*): meaning the disbeliever.

The first: it completes His statement *"Allan najmaʿa ʿiẓāmah"*, meaning: "Yes, We will assemble them." This is the view of al-Akhfash.

The second: it is a new statement after the first has ended, expressing wonder: *Balā qādirīn*, etc. In this there are two possibilities:

One: "Yes, We are able to put together his joints and return them for the resurrection in a new creation." This is the view of Jarīr ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.

The second: "Yes, We are able to make his hand, with which he eats and works, into the hoof of a donkey or the sole of a camel, so that he eats only with his mouth and does nothing with his hand." This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah.

﴿Bal yurīdu l-insānu liyafjura amāmah﴾ (*Rather, man desires to continue in sin ahead of him*). In this there are four interpretations:

The first: its meaning is that he advances the sin and postpones repentance. This is the view of al-Qāsim ibn al-Walīd.

The second: he goes forward ahead of him, not turning away from wickedness. This is the view of al-Ḥasan.

The third: rather, he desires to commit sins in this world due to the strength of his hope, and does not remember death. This is the view of al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The fourth: rather, he desires to deny the Resurrection and not be punished with the Fire. This is the meaning of the view of Ibn Zayd.

It may also bear a fifth interpretation: rather, he desires to deny what is in the Hereafter just as he denied what is in this world. He means: if he denied me regarding what I mentioned.

The first: it means it became weak and was broken at death. This is the view of ʿAbdullāh ibn Abī Isḥāq.

The second: it stared and opened its eye in terror at the sight of the Angel of Death. Al-Farrāʾ recited:

That is: do not be terrified by the horror of the wounds.

The second reading: with a *kasrah* on the *rāʾ*, recited by the rest of the readers. In its interpretation there are two possibilities:

The first: lightning dazzled his eyes on the Day of Resurrection. This is the view of Ashhab al-ʿUqaylī. Al-Aʿshā said:

*"I used to see in the face of Mayya a glimpse, so I was dazzled, overcome, in my place."*

The second: the splitting of the sight. This is the view of Abū ʿUbayda, who recited the words of al-Kilābī:

*"When Ibn ʿUmayr came to me desiring [my camels], I gave him she-camels, tawny, and he was dazzled."*

The first: that He joined them in their rising from the west, [black and rolled up,] dark and bound together.

The second: He joined them in the going away of their light by the eclipse, so that the darkness of the earth upon its people is complete. This is related from Ibn Shajarah.

The third: He joined them in the sea until they become the great Fire of God.

﴿Yaqūlu l-insānu yawma'idhin ayna l-mafarr﴾ (*Man will say on that Day, "Where is the escape?"*): meaning, where is the refuge? The poet said:

*"Where shall I flee while the rams butt, and what ram, swerving away from them, will be disgraced?"*

It may bear two possibilities:

The first: "Where is the escape?" from God, out of shame before Him.

The second: "Where is the escape?" from Hell, out of fear of it.

This statement from man may bear two possibilities:

The first: that it is from the disbeliever specifically, from the plain of the Resurrection, not from the believer, because of the believer's confidence in the good news of his Lord.

The second: that it is from the statement of both the believer and the disbeliever at the coming of the Hour, due to the horror of what they witness of it.(p-154)

This statement may bear two possibilities:

The first: it is from God's statement to man, when he says, "Where is the escape?" God says to him, *"Kallā, lā wazar"* (*No! There is no refuge*).

The second: it is from the statement of man when he knows that there is no escape for him; he says to himself, *"Kallā, lā wazar"* (*No! There is no refuge*).

*"Kallā, lā wazar"* has four interpretations:

The first: meaning there is no refuge from the Fire. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās.

The second: no fortress. This is the view of Ibn Masʿūd.

The third: no mountain. This is the view of al-Ḥasan.

The fourth: no escape. This is the view of Ibn Jubayr.

﴿Ilā rabbika yawma'idhin al-mustaqarr﴾ (*To your Lord, that Day, is the place of rest*). In this there are two possibilities:

The first: that *al-mustaqarr* is the final end. This is the view of Qatādah.

The second: that it is the settling of the people of Paradise in Paradise and the people of the Fire in the Fire. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

The first: what he sent ahead before his death of good or evil, which he will know after his death. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd.

The second: what he sent ahead of disobedience and kept back of obedience. This is the view of Qatādah.

The third: by the first of his deeds and the last of them. This is the view of Mujāhid.

The fourth: by what he sent ahead of evil and kept back of good. This is the view of ʿIkrimah.

The fifth: by what he sent ahead of an obligation and kept back of an obligation. This is the view of al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

It may bear a sixth: what he sent ahead for his worldly life, and what he kept back for his afterlife.

The second: no fortress. This is the view of Ibn Masʿūd.

The third: no mountain. This is the view of al-Ḥasan.

The second: He would hasten to repeat it when it was revealed to him, out of his love for it and the sweetness of it on his tongue. So he was forbidden from this until it had been gathered, because some of it is connected to other parts. This is what 'Amir al-Sha'bi said.(p-156)

﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation.﴾ On this there are three views:

One: Upon Us is its collection in your heart, so that you may recite it with your tongue. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said.

The second: Upon Us is its preservation and its arrangement. This is what Qatadah said.

The third: Upon Us is that We gather it for you until you establish it in your heart. This is what al-Dahhak said.

﴿So when We have recited it, follow its recitation.﴾ On this there are three views:

One: So when We have explained it, act upon what is in it. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said.

The second: So when We have sent it down, listen to its recitation. This is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: So when it is recited to you, follow its laws and rulings. This is what Qatadah said.

The third: Upon Us is that We recompense on the Day of Resurrection for what it contains of promise or threat. This is what al-Hasan said.

One: You love the reward of this world and leave the reward of the Hereafter. This is what Muqatil said.

The second: You love the deeds of this world and leave the deeds of the Hereafter.

The second: Joyful. This is what Mujahid said.

The third: Flourishing. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said.

The fourth: Joyful and glad. This is what 'Ikrimah said.

The second: Changed. This is what al-Suddi said.

*I swear by God with the utmost oath: God has not left anything aimless.*

﴿Was he not a drop of semen emitted?﴾ On this there are three opinions:

First: the meaning of yumnā is "poured forth," which is why Minā was so named for the shedding of blood there.

Second: it means "comes into being and is created." From this is the saying of Yazīd ibn ʿĀmir:

*Take your path, walking without humility, until you meet what the one who promises (al-māni) promises you.*

Third: it means "mingles," that is, the mingling of the man's fluid with the woman's fluid.

﴿Then he became a clinging clot﴾ meaning that after the drop he became a clot.

﴿Then He shaped and proportioned﴾ This may bear two meanings:

One: He created from the wombs before birth, and proportioned after it, when strength is complete and movement is perfected.

Second: He created bodies and proportioned them for actions, so that He made for every limb a function. And God knows best.
